title: Git & the Pull-Request Workflow
summary: Git records code changes so you can review work and return to earlier versions.

subtopics.title: Main idea
subtopics.explanation: A repository is a folder whose file history is tracked by Git. It includes the project files and the record of changes. It is like a notebook that keeps earlier drafts, not just the latest page. A repository may live on your computer and on a hosting service such as GitHub. For example, clone the repository to make a local working copy before editing a feature.

subtopics.title: Important part
subtopics.explanation: A commit saves a set of changes with a message explaining their purpose. It is like a labeled checkpoint you can return to or compare later. Keep commits focused so reviewers can understand them. Before committing, inspect the changed files and make sure generated secrets or unrelated edits are not included. For example, commit a focused change with a message that says what the edit accomplishes.

subtopics.title: How it works
subtopics.explanation: A branch is a named line of work based on a previous commit. You can change files on a branch without changing the main branch. It is like making a copy of a draft for an experiment. Branches make parallel work easier, but they do not automatically prevent conflicts when two changes edit the same lines. For example, create a branch for a task so unfinished work does not alter the shared main branch.

subtopics.title: A useful detail
subtopics.explanation: A merge combines changes from one branch into another. Git may do this automatically, or it may ask you to resolve a conflict when both branches changed the same area. It is like combining two edited pages and choosing what to keep where they disagree. Run the project checks after resolving conflicts. For example, resolve a merge conflict by comparing both intended changes, not by choosing a side blindly.

subtopics.title: Good practice
subtopics.explanation: A diff shows the lines added, removed, or changed. Read it before committing and again before opening a pull request. It is like proofreading the exact edits rather than relying on memory. Review helps catch accidental files, debug output, and changes that do not match the intended task. For example, review the diff to catch a generated file or secret before sharing the branch.

foundations.overview: Git records how files in a project change over time. A repository is the project history; commits are saved snapshots, and branches let people work on separate changes. Think of a commit as a labeled checkpoint in a shared notebook. Git helps teams review work and recover earlier versions, but it cannot decide whether a change is correct or safe.
foundations.whyItMatters: Git gives teams a reviewable history and a way to work in parallel. Understanding local commits, branches, merges, and pushes prevents confusion about which changes are saved or shared.
foundations.browserPerspective: Not browser-specific, but it's how the code that becomes your frontend gets integrated and shipped.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Feature branches, PR review, resolving merge conflicts, reverting a bad deploy, and reading git blame/log to understand history.
foundations.businessImpact: Good PR hygiene speeds delivery and reduces production incidents; bad Git practice causes lost work and broken main branches.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Small reviewable PRs, meaningful commits, and clean history make the codebase maintainable and onboarding faster.
foundations.performanceImpact: N/A directly, but CI runs on PRs and gates merges, tightening the feedback loop.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Rebase is always better than merge.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Rebase gives linear history but rewrites commits — never rebase a branch others are working on; merge is safer for shared branches.
Large PRs are slower to review and hide bugs; small, focused PRs merge faster and safer.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A branch is a separate copy of the repository that can never conflict.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Branches can edit the same lines; Git may need a person to resolve the merge.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A commit automatically uploads work for teammates.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A commit records a local snapshot; pushing or opening a pull request shares it.

keyTakeaways: A repository is a folder whose file history is tracked by Git.
A commit saves a set of changes with a message explaining their purpose.
A branch is a named line of work based on a previous commit.
A merge combines changes from one branch into another.
A diff shows the lines added, removed, or changed.
